headings.text: Do not destroy the volumes unless you need a complete reboot

blocks.html:
Run an instance for at most ~3 months. For safety, we recommend a maximum deployment time of about three months per instance. A Deploy App instance's containers are not meant to be updated during a server's lifetime — you patch by redeploying a fresh instance, not by maintaining a long-lived one. The model is one operation, one server: a new operation gets a new instance. This also minimizes data build-up and configuration drift over time.

Day-2 operations for a Docker Compose Deploy App instance: keeping it patched, understanding its short design lifetime, the one command never to run on a live instance, and backups. All of this is grounded in the legacy docker-rasenmaeher-integration README. For initial standup see Deploy with Docker Compose; for failure modes see Troubleshooting & teardown.

Updating an instance

Note the design intent: there are no in-place upgrades in the long-running sense. An instance is meant to be patched by redeploying, and is expected to be refreshed rather than maintained indefinitely.

If you, however, want try to update, do it the below way.

Update the repository, re-sync submodules to the checked-out version, pull the matching images, and recreate the services:

git pull
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d

If you ever cloned or checked out without --recurse-submodules, the git submodule update --init --recursive step also repairs that.

Design lifetime

A Deploy App instance has a design lifetime of 1–2 months, with a recommended operational ceiling of about 3 months (see the banner above). The short lifetime is deliberate: it forces instance refreshing, which avoids accumulated maintenance, persistence, and user-management drift.

If you genuinely need an instance to outlive that window, you can extend the certificate validity — but this is not recommended and has security implications. If you do it, you take responsibility for reading through all Dockerfiles and compositions to understand exactly how things are built and for applying security updates into the containers yourself.

CFSSL_CA_EXPIRY="8800h"            # hours; 8800h is ~366 days
CFSSL_SIGN_DEFAULT_EXPIRY="8800h"  # hours; 8800h is ~366 days

These set the CFSSL CA and default signing expiry. Leaving them at defaults keeps the instance within its intended short life.

Once again: Do not run an instance for time longer that 3 months.

Do not destroy the volumes unless you need a complete reboot

# !DO NOT DO! on a live instance
docker compose down -v

docker compose down -v deletes the persistent volumes — the certificates, users, and databases — and you will have to re-add all users and re-enroll all devices. Use plain docker compose down (no -v) to stop the stack while keeping state. The -v form is only for intentionally resetting dev environments or before the integration test suite (which requires a clean database). See Troubleshooting & teardown for the full teardown discussion.

Backups

Not yet documented. A supported backup/restore procedure for a Docker Compose instance — which named volumes to snapshot (CFSSL/CA material, postgres pg_data, TAK tak_data) and a tested restore path — is still to be written. The README documents no backup flow today; given the short design lifetime, the project's stance is to refresh/redeploy rather than maintain long-lived instances, so plan around disposability rather than long-term restore.

What the sources do make clear is that the persistent volumes hold everything that matters (CA/certificates, users, databases), and that destroying them (down -v) is irreversible — so any backup strategy must capture those volumes while the stack is down or quiesced.

Monitoring during operation

Keep an eye on the audit and security logs throughout the instance's life — certificate lifecycle events, auth failures, and the compromise indicators. See Audit logging & observability for the log model, where logs live, and the health-check endpoints.

Organization-wide operational and contribution conventions are deferred to the Community & Standards page (in Contribute to Project).
